newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak leaders say NATO summit decision unfair.
newsitem.headline: Slovak leaders say NATO summit decision unfair.

text.p: Slovak leaders on Wednesday lamented their country's exclusion from invitations to join NATO, suggesting that the decision of the 16-member alliance was unfair.

The Bratislava daily Sme quoted Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar as saying the decision to invite Poland, Hungary, and former federation partners the Czech Republic to start negotiations for entry to NATO was not objective.

"It must be said that many states applied different measures in assessing eligibility for membership -- one for themselves, another for our neighbours, and another for us," Meciar was quoted as saying.

Slovakia has repeatedly come under fire from the United States, NATO allies, and the European Union for alleged foot-dragging on democratic reforms and creating a transparent economy -- warnings Meciar has patently rejected.
Military leaders said they would continue to participate in the alliance's Partnership for Peace (PfP) programme which sets up training and joint exercises with non-member countries.
"I am sorry and sad, but not frustrated," Slovak Chief of the General Staff General Jozef Tuchyna told a news conference.
An official government statement published in the pro-government daily Slovenska Republika made no mention of Slovakia's exclusion in Tuesday's NATO communique.
But it reiterated the government line expressing its willingness to continue cooperation with the alliance.

"Slovakia will continue its intensive cooperation both with current NATO members but also with those central and eastern European countries invited at the Madrid summit to start talks on entry to the alliance," the statement said.

While NATO's official declaration agreed in Madrid left the door open to all European countries who fulfil NATO's requirements for membership, it made special reference to Romania and Slovenia as potential candidates.
"We recognise with great interest and take account of the positive developments towards democracy and the rule of law in a number of southeastern European countries, especially Romania and Slovenia,"
Nothing was said about Slovakia, despite the republic's one-time frontrunner status soon after its split with the Czech Republic in 1993.
Opposition parties' reaction to the apparent snub placed the blame squarely on Meciar's government.
Opposition leader Jozef Moravcik, a former foreign minister and prime minister, said Meciar was responsible for Slovakia not even being mentioned as a future candidate.
"It is the shocking reputation of the Meciar government which is totally unacceptable for western countries," Moravcik said.
But Meciar allies rejected the criticsm.
"This was not our fiasco," Eva Zelenayova, a parliamentary deputy for Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), told the independent radio Twist.
"If one follows foreign politics one can see that this was the result of political interests of certain powers, Zelenayova said. "This puts to shame those who took this decision."
She did not elaborate on which powers she meant.
General Tuchyna said a detailed analysis would be neccessary to determine the responsiblity for Slovakia's failure to enter NATO, but declined to place the blame on any individual institutions.
"This will in no way deter us from continuing our activities in the PfP and other tasks of integrating our army in western structures," Tuchyna said.
"The Slovak army fulfilled its tasks according to the government programme," Tuchyna said. "The rest is not in my competence."
